papers.relied_on: Narrative review as source for C-peptide use in classification and insulin withdrawal (rows 6, 31, 32), for renal clearance as an interpretation limit (row 28), and for assay and workflow burden.
papers.full_text_shows: Review (PubMed search to Aug 2012; no systematic method or grading) says random C-peptide with concurrent glucose >8 mmol/L was the best classifier in one large study and is 'likely' sufficient in most situations; stimulated <0.6 nmol/L suggests marked deficiency, <0.2 nmol/L absolute deficiency. For insulin withdrawal it says the role is mainly to exclude absolute deficiency, and that the withdrawal studies (Table 3) are short, use lax glycaemic targets and rarely include low C-peptide groups. About half of C-peptide is renally cleared, so blood values are falsely elevated in renal impairment and correction methods are poorly validated; assay standardisation has not been achieved, mainly at higher concentrations.
papers.quote: Mechanisms to correct for renal function when measuring C-peptide have been suggested, but are currently poorly validated
papers.key_numbers: Stimulated C-peptide <0.6 nmol/L (fasting <0.25) suggests marked deficiency; <0.2 nmol/L (fasting <0.08) absolute deficiency; preserved C-peptide after ketoacidosis: fasting >0.33 or glucagon >0.5 nmol/L, about 50% insulin-free at 1 year in one mostly non-Caucasian cohort; about 50% renal clearance, about 5% excreted unchanged; 2-h urine C-peptide:creatinine <0.2 nmol/mmol 96% sensitive, 98% specific (Exeter, n=70 vs 145).
papers.role_in_work: Primary review source for row 6 thresholds, row 28 renal caveat, rows 31 and 32 workflow; stands behind D1, D2, D4, D5, D6 and S entries.
papers.design: Narrative review with PubMed search to August 2012; not a guideline.
papers.population_and_size: Adults and children with diabetes, mainly European studies; no pooled sample.
papers.measure_type: C-peptide: random (non-fasting, glucose >8 mmol/L), fasting, glucagon- and mixed-meal-stimulated, post-meal urine C-peptide:creatinine; not insulin.
papers.assay_or_platform: Generic discussion of immunoassays; says standardisation is not achieved and results near thresholds may not be comparable across methods.
papers.quality_note: Pre-2013 review with expert opinion in places ('likely'); funding NIHR and Wellcome. It has no passage on secretagogue hypoglycaemia in kidney disease (not found in the text), so row 28 S rests on judgement. Its thresholds differ from Holt 2021 (stimulated 0.6 and 0.2 nmol/L vs 600 and 80 pmol/L random).

papers.relied_on: Consensus text as the guideline source that recommends random C-peptide for uncertain type beyond 3 years and requires it before insulin discontinuation (rows 6 and 31 D1, D3, D5, D6).
papers.full_text_shows: The text says a random C-peptide with concurrent glucose within 5 h of eating is recommended beyond 3 years where type is uncertain, and that in insulin-treated people it should always be done before insulin discontinuation. The Figure 1 note adds thresholds (>=600 pmol/L circumstances do not matter; <80 pmol/L no repeat; 200-600 usually T1D or MODY but can be insulin-treated T2D; no test within 2 weeks of a hyperglycaemic emergency). Autoantibodies (GAD first) are the primary investigation. For suspected monogenic diabetes it says to test antibodies and C-peptide and to consider genetic testing only if antibodies are negative and non-fasting C-peptide >200 pmol/L. Renal impairment is named only as a confounder of the urinary C-peptide:creatinine ratio. The authors state the report is consensus opinion because evidence is incomplete.
papers.quote: Where a person is treated with insulin, this test should always be performed prior to insulin discontinuation to exclude severe insulin deficiency.
papers.key_numbers: Thresholds 600, 200-600 and 80 pmol/L; >40% of adults who develop T1D after age 30 are first treated as T2D; reclassification in 11% of adult-onset diabetes with 3+ years' duration (ref 31, primary study not identified in the corpus text); urine C-peptide:creatinine <0.2 nmol/mol (as printed) for severe deficiency.
papers.role_in_work: Guideline-level source for D3 (4 for the insulin-discontinuation decision), D1 and D2 (consensus), D5, D6 and the row 6 path to viability.
papers.design: ADA/EASD consensus report; authors summarise literature, peer review and public comment; no formal grading.
papers.population_and_size: Adults with suspected or established type 1 diabetes; flowchart based on White European data.
papers.measure_type: C-peptide: random (non-fasting) plasma with concurrent glucose within 5 h of eating; urinary C-peptide:creatinine as alternative; not insulin.
papers.assay_or_platform: Not specified; plasma preferred, urine confounded by renal impairment.
papers.quality_note: Consensus opinion by the authors' own statement; the 'must' sentence is a precaution before stopping insulin, not a trial result. The flowchart is for newly diagnosed adults and White European data. The 11% reclassification figure cannot be traced from the Foteinopoulou paper (6.8% overall).

papers.relied_on: Survey as evidence that insulin and C-peptide assays are not standardised, used to score D4 at 3 (rows 6 and 31) and 2 (row 5), with the figures 'inter-system CV 24.5%, 5.7% after recalibration' quoted from the abstract.
papers.full_text_shows: The local text has no abstract or tables; 24.5% and 5.7% are not found in it. It gives, for C-peptide, inter-laboratory CV 13.6-21.8% and inter-measurement-system CV 20.1-31.6% against a desirable 8.3%, worst for the lowest-concentration sample (31.6%); intra-system CV was acceptable (mean 6.6%). After recalibration all C-peptide inter-system CVs met 8.3%. For insulin inter-system CV was 10.7-58.3% (44.1% after recalibration at the low sample), and no insulin reference procedure is listed in JCTLM.
papers.quote: inter-measurement system %CVs ranging from 10.7% to 58.3% for insulin and from 20.1% to 31.6% for C-peptide
papers.key_numbers: 94 laboratories, 5 pooled sera; C-peptide inter-lab CV 13.6-21.8%, inter-system 20.1-31.6%, desirable 8.3%; insulin inter-lab 8.4-64.3%, inter-system 10.7-58.3%, desirable 10.6%; 91 laboratories reported insulin, 88 C-peptide.
papers.role_in_work: Only non-US assay-standardisation survey behind D4 for rows 5, 6, 31.
papers.design: Cross-sectional external-quality style survey with recalibration analysis.
papers.population_and_size: 94 laboratories in China, 5 pooled leftover serum samples (Siemens-measured at Beijing Hospital), 6 repeats each.
papers.measure_type: Serum insulin and C-peptide concentration (analytical study; no post-meal or stimulated protocol).
papers.assay_or_platform: Roche, Siemens, Abbott, Beckman, Snibe, Mindray immunoassays.
papers.quality_note: Chinese laboratories, so anchor 20 applies (non-US, confidence cap medium); only two samples used for recalibration; sample concentrations not given in the local text; the 24.5% and 5.7% figures could not be verified (text partial). Low-concentration samples were worst for both analytes, which does not fit the V3 statement that the low end is less affected.

papers.relied_on: ADA Standards 2026 section 2 as guideline source: Figure 2.1 C-peptide note (rows 6, 31), no C-peptide recommendation for MODY (row 7), ketosis-prone diabetes (row 32), slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes (row 47) and staging (row 49); 40% misdiagnosis figure (row 31 D7).
papers.full_text_shows: The C-peptide statements are in the footnote to the Figure 2.1 flowchart (web text), copied from Holt 2021; they are not in the numbered graded recommendations (2.5 only says to classify). No numbered recommendation or text names C-peptide for MODY (2.29b is genetic testing), ketosis-prone diabetes (only 'generally transient' insulin need), LADA (term acceptable, no C-peptide criterion) or staging (2.6-2.8b use autoantibodies and glucose). The text says misdiagnosis can occur in up to 40% of adults with new type 1 diabetes. Low C-peptide appears only as a late-stage marker and in fulminant checkpoint-inhibitor diabetes.
papers.quote: Where a person is insulin treated, C-peptide must be measured prior to insulin discontinuation to exclude severe insulin deficiency.
papers.key_numbers: 600 pmol/L (1.8 ng/mL), 80 pmol/L (0.24 ng/mL), 2-week rule; 40% misdiagnosis; monogenic diabetes in under 5% of diabetes.
papers.role_in_work: Second guideline source for D3 on rows 6, 7, 31, 32, 47, 49 and D1 on row 49.
papers.design: Annual guideline (Standards of Care), PMC web-page version.
papers.population_and_size: Adults and children with or at risk of diabetes; guideline, no sample.
papers.measure_type: C-peptide: random non-fasting with concurrent glucose within 5 h of eating (Figure 2.1 note); post-load C-peptide not addressed.
papers.quality_note: Web text, not verbatim PDF; the C-peptide advice is an ungraded figure note, not a graded recommendation; flowchart is based on White European data and newly diagnosed adults. Duality-of-interest information is only linked.

papers.relied_on: Abstract numbers (859 tested, 6.8% reclassified, 1.5% stopped insulin) as the reclassification cohort behind D2 and D8 for row 6.
papers.full_text_shows: Single-centre routine clinic programme (Edinburgh) in people with clinician-diagnosed T1D of 3+ years who all started insulin within 3 years. Random non-fasting serum C-peptide on Abbott Architect; a value at or above about 200 pmol/L (symbol lost in extraction) triggered antibodies, T1 genetic risk score and genetic testing. 114 of 859 (13.2%) triggered; yield rose with age at diagnosis (2.5% under 18, 15.4% at 18-30, 25.9% over 30). 58 (6.8%) were reclassified (44 T2D, 14 monogenic); 13 (1.5%) stayed off insulin and 16 (1.9%) gained from co-therapy, with no severe hypoglycaemia or DKA reported. The threshold was pragmatic, and Abbott and Roche values differ (Abbott = 0.8755 x Roche - 40.6, so Abbott 200 is Roche 269).
papers.quote: The cause of diabetes was reclassified in 58 individuals (6.8% of the tested cohort).
papers.key_numbers: 953 eligible, 859 tested (90%); 114 (13.2%) at or above threshold; 58 reclassified (6.8%); 13 stopped insulin (1.5%); testing programme cost about 27 pounds per person tested.
papers.role_in_work: The one implementation cohort behind row 6 D2 (3) and D8 (3, anchor 19 reclassification rate).
papers.design: Prospective single-centre observational service evaluation, no control group, no ethics approval (service development).
papers.population_and_size: 859 adults tested, hospital diabetes clinic, predominantly Caucasian, clinician-diagnosed T1D 3+ years.
papers.measure_type: C-peptide: random non-fasting serum with concurrent glucose.
papers.assay_or_platform: Abbott ARCHITECT i2000SR (CV 2.9-4.1%); Roche conversion given.
papers.quality_note: Reclassification depends on a downstream antibody, genetic-score and sequencing work-up, not C-peptide alone; no comparison with antibody-first testing; authors say the population limits transfer and the cut-off is pragmatic. The 11% figure in Holt is not printed in this text. No conflict related to the work; one author has pharma honoraria.

papers.relied_on: 14% misclassification by UK clinical criteria in insulin-treated adults, used as an anchor for the share with unclear type in the row 6 D7 chain.
papers.full_text_shows: 601 white European insulin-treated adults with 5+ years' diabetes, recruited by letter (volunteers) in three UK centres; 514 (86%) correctly classified by the UK guideline against a urinary C-peptide:creatinine gold standard (2 h after the largest meal). Of 87 misclassified, 57 (66%) were labelled T1D but made substantial insulin and 30 (34%) were labelled T2D but severely deficient. The authors state the 14% would be much lower across all people with diabetes.
papers.quote: most (n = 57, 66%, Figure 2) were misclassified as having type 1 diabetes and were producing substantial endogenous insulin
papers.key_numbers: 601 included; 86% (95% CI 83-88) correct; 87 misclassified; gold standard UCPCR <0.2 nmol/mmol at 5+ years and insulin within 3 years.
papers.role_in_work: Epidemiological anchor for the unclear-type share in the row 6 D7 chain (V7).
papers.design: Cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study of clinical criteria against C-peptide.
papers.population_and_size: 601 white European (and 30 Asian) insulin-treated adults, 5+ years' duration, UK.
papers.measure_type: C-peptide: post-meal (2 h) urinary C-peptide:creatinine ratio; not serum random, not insulin.
papers.assay_or_platform: Exeter biochemistry laboratory UCPCR assay (not detailed in the text read).
papers.quality_note: UK, volunteer responders, insulin-treated only, so it fits the insulin-treated denominator but not US practice or all diabetes; 'misclassified' means against the UK algorithm, not 'type uncertain to the clinician'. Supports the D7 share as an assumption, not a measurement.

papers.relied_on: 2016 NHIS split of diagnosed diabetes by type (5.8% T1, 90.9% T2, 3.3% other) as a US denominator for row 6 D7.
papers.full_text_shows: Self-reported, 33,028 adults, response rate 54.3%; 3,519 with diabetes: T1D 0.55% (1.3 million), T2D 8.6% (21.0 million), other 0.31%. T1D means self-reported T1 plus current insulin use; self-reported T1 without insulin (n=182), unknown type and refusals were put in T2D. Type is not validated and the authors say insulin-secretion tests are unsuitable for surveys. It gives no count of insulin-treated adults with unclear type.
papers.quote: the estimated prevalences of diagnosed type 1 and type 2 diabetes were 0.55% (corresponding to 1.3 million U.S. adults)
papers.key_numbers: 1.3 million T1D adults (2016); 21.0 million T2D; 211 of 3,519 classified T1.
papers.role_in_work: Denominator source (type split) for row 6 D7; U1 uses the later CDC 1.8 million figure for T1D.
papers.measure_type: Not a measurement study (no insulin or C-peptide test); epidemiology only.
papers.quality_note: Self-reported, unvalidated type, 2016 data; supports the type split but not the uncertain-type or retest shares.

papers.relied_on: Clinical-model study cited as using C-peptide as the reference standard (row 6 D2) and as showing clinical features alone discriminate well (rows 6 and 31 D8).
papers.full_text_shows: Models built on 1,352 white European UK adults (179 T1D) diagnosed at 18-50 years; outcome defined by insulin within 3 years plus non-fasting C-peptide <200 pmol/L (T1D) or >600 pmol/L at 5+ years (T2D). Age and BMI alone gave AUC 0.904 in development and 0.865 in external validation (n=582); adding GADA, IA-2A and genetic risk score reached 0.97. In the 71 hardest cases antibodies alone gave 0.72 and genetic risk score alone 0.89. C-peptide is the outcome, never a predictor, so the paper cannot show what C-peptide adds.
papers.quote: Type 1 diabetes: Insulin treatment within ≤3 years of diabetes diagnosis and severe insulin deficiency (non-fasting C-peptide <200 pmol/L).
papers.key_numbers: AUC 0.904 clinical, 0.97 five-predictor (development); external 0.865 and 0.930 (clinical, clinical+GADA); 37 (2.7%) undefinable outcome at C-peptide 200-600 pmol/L; 87% of C-peptide samples non-fasting.
papers.role_in_work: Shows C-peptide is the reference standard and clinical models approximate it; supports D8 not above 3 and row 31 D8 at 2.
papers.design: Diagnostic model development with internal and external validation, cross-sectional.
papers.population_and_size: 1,352 development, 582 external, white European adults aged 18-50 at diagnosis.
papers.measure_type: C-peptide: random non-fasting (87%), some fasting (x2.5) or 90-min mixed-meal, used as outcome definition only.
papers.assay_or_platform: Roche electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (development cohort); different assays in the external cohort.
papers.quality_note: Circular for the question of what C-peptide adds; white European, 18-50 only; time to insulin self-reported; antibodies and BMI measured about 13 years after diagnosis.

Jones 2013 also says standardisation has not been achieved and results near thresholds may not be comparable. D4 3 stays defensible if thresholds are far from the cutoffs (thresholds 80, 200, 600 pmol/L are 2.5 to 3 fold apart), so this is a boundary call. notes: Only two proposals change a score (row 6 D4 and row 31 D4, 3 to 2, low confidence, together); everything else is confirmation or null. Row 6 and 31 path to viability: an agreed assay calibration is supported as a small assay-type step by C080 (recalibration removed most C-peptide discordance); row 28 path unchanged. Assumptions: the lost symbol in the C169 threshold ('C-peptide 200 pmol/L') is read as 'at or above'; C169 is an accepted-manuscript PDF extraction. C080 text lacks abstract and tables, so 24.5% and 5.7% were not verified. Several score entries (U4/U5 D5 and D6 ordering and consequence claims, V18 D5) rest on judgement; the texts do not say who orders the test beyond C169 (hospital diabetes clinic). Current scores were read from the entries in usecases/scoring/*.json; entries with original_score and correction were taken at their corrected value. Tool calls used: 30.
